summary:
Sol Survivor is a free, browser-based game in which kids aged 7–12 keep a Mars outpost alive for 15 sols. Players balance three resources (Power, Life Support, and Radiation Shield) with only ten work hours per sol, so every repair costs something else. There is no free "safe" choice: the problems come from real missions, such as Apollo 13's mismatched CO2 filter, the 2018 dust storm that silenced Opportunity, and an air leak on the International Space Station.

Real NASA open data drives the game. The solar event on Sol 12 is an actual flare from NASA's DONKI database, and its recorded strength determines how hard it hits the player's shield. Radiation dose rates are based on measurements from the ISS and from Curiosity on Mars.

What makes Sol Survivor different is the Black Box. After the mission, players change one past decision, predict what will happen, and watch the game replay the mission with that single change, showing both outcomes side by side and explaining why. Kids practice the scientific method (predict, test, compare, explain) and learn from failure instead of being punished by it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sol Survivor is a browser game in which a child aged 7–12 runs a Mars outpost alone for 15 sols. Three resources must be kept alive (Power, Life Support and Radiation Shield) with only ten work hours per sol. Each sol brings a fault at one of seven stations (greenhouse, shelter, battery room, airlock, solar field and others). The player walks there in first person, sees the problem, picks one of several fixes, and does the work by hand, for example wiping dust off a solar panel. Results stay visible in the world, and postponed faults visibly get worse.

Play it here: https://alicagriyildiz.github.io/sol-survivor/

HOW IT TEACHES TRADE-OFFS

There is no free option. Cleaning the panels raises power but costs hours, air and radiation dose. Reinforcing the shelter on Sol 6 costs time and power today and pays off during the solar event on Sol 12. Most problems are based on real missions: Apollo 13's mismatched CO2 filter, the 2018 global dust storm that ended Opportunity's mission, perchlorate in Martian soil found by Phoenix, and an air leak on the ISS. Each sol ends with a short "What really happened?" note and its source.

THE BLACK BOX

After the mission, win or lose, the player opens the Black Box, changes one past decision, predicts the result, and the game replays the entire mission with that single change. Both outcomes are shown side by side with a plain-language explanation of the cause. The simulation is fully deterministic, so the replay is a real recalculation, not a guess. If no single change would have saved the mission, the game says so. Children practice the scientific method (predict, test, compare, explain) and learn from failure without being punished for it.

REAL DATA IN THE MECHANICS

The Sol 12 solar event is a real flare from NASA DONKI. Its recorded class sets the shield damage and the dose. Dose rates are based on ISS dosimetry from OSDR RadLab and on Curiosity RAD surface measurements. Storm power loss follows published values from the 2018 dust storm. Data is archived and embedded in the game, not live, and an in-game Data screen lists every source. Repair times and costs are simplified game design.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS BALANCED

Automated players ran 200 missions each. A player who does nothing wins 0%, one who always picks the cheapest fix wins 3%, a random player 19.5%, and a careful player 83.5%. There is no single dominant strategy. A harder Commander level removes all hints. The project has 104 automated tests. It has not yet been tested with children; that is our next step.

IMPACT

No download, no account, works on a phone, fits one class period, and is available in Turkish and English. The code is open source (MIT) so others can add Moon or ISS scenarios.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, Vitest, GitHub Pages. 3D models: Kenney Space Kit (CC0). The code was written with AI assistance (Claude Code). The game concept, rules, scenarios, balance targets and testing were designed and directed by the team.
